extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys, examiners), IP judges, policy makers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for determining when a disclosure (including via new media) constitutes prior art that destroys novelty or affects inventive step for patent applications. Covers evidentiary, temporal, geographical, and confidentiality aspects across jurisdictions (Sweden, Switzerland, and EPO comparisons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evident abuse requires mala fide intent
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute an 'evident abuse' the abuser must have acted mala fide — i.e. had intent to destroy the novelty of the invention or at least been aware that his measures could lead to such result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a subjective requisite: abuse must be intentional or made with awareness of likely prejudice to novelty (see Swedish Patents Appeal Court decision cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing in public may be non-prejudicial if constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing a commercially-available object containing the invention on public roads is not necessarily considered to destroy novelty under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions: (i) tests are necessary to finish the invention; (ii) all reasonable measures are taken to restrict the public's ability to obtain information about the invention; and (iii) tests are not carried out longer or to a larger extent than defendable given the character of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of whether disclosure is public depends on recipient/control
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a disclosure is public must be determined case-by-case, considering number of people who received the information, their relation to the inventor, and any explicit or implicit confidentiality agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A generally applied rule: if a large or indefinite group could have had the opportunity to receive the information, the disclosure is regarded as having taken place; it is irrelevant whether anyone actually used that opportunity. The critical question is whether the inventor controls the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient's ability to understand is immaterial (theoretical comprehension suffices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that a recipient theoretically can comprehend the invention is enough for destroying novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle the recipient's actual understanding is without importance; same principle applies as for reverse engineering: theoretical ability to understand suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule: same standards apply across media (including new media)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same rules/principles for prior art, novelty and inventive step should apply irrespective of the medium used to disclose the information (paper, oral, electronic networks, Internet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New media introduce evidentiary issues but do not justify different substantive standards for novelty/non-obviousness; harmonisation of detailed rules/guidelines is desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential electronic communication preserves confidentiality when access is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Information subject to a confidentiality agreement and made accessible only to a limited, identified set of recipients (for example by encryption and/or passwords) should satisfy the requirement of confidentiality and not count as public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors may use electronic means provided normal/proper precautions preserve confidentiality. Passwords and encryption act as electronic keys: if access is limited, disclosure remains confidential; cracked encryption or unauthorized disclosure may nonetheless be treated as publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure is irrelevant — absolute worldwide novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement for novelty should have general (universal) application; geographical limitations are unsuitable in view of worldwide electronic communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute novelty is demanded; the place where a disclosure occurs is not relevant for novelty assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of internet disclosures: whole-day and time-zone issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure on the Internet is made available instantaneously worldwide but may give rise to different disclosure dates in different countries due to time differences (whole-day rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration must be given to time-zone differences when deciding whether the disclosure occurred before the filing date. Duration of posting generally not decisive; practical approach: disclosure is prejudicial if sufficient for a skilled person to understand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of electronic availability not decisive if skilled person can understand
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not practical to qualify a disclosure as prejudicial or not depending on the duration of availability, as long as it is sufficient for a skilled person to understand the information according to the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open question whether time needed for understanding could be replaced by time needed for downloading; duration alone should not determine prejudicial effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for prior art disclosure lies with the party asserting it
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof that a prior disclosure is in fact prior art falls on the party seeking to apply such disclosure as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can collect and save information in permanent form with adequate evidence of the disclosure date; courts evaluate evidence reliability at their discretion; electronic manipulation possibilities should be treated similarly to other evidence-manipulation risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and inventive step are primary patentability issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for novelty and non-obviousness (inventive step) are the most frequent and important issues in examination and litigation, and therefore of great importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmonisation worldwide of the concept of novelty is highly desirable; detailed guidelines for internet disclosures (conditions for being publicly available, establishing time) would be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: state of the art / what counts as disclosure (Swiss Art.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: State of the art comprises everything that before the filing- or priority date has been made available to the public by written or oral description, by use, or in any other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location, language, time gap, or medium of disclosure do not matter under Art.7(2) PatG; for assessment of content the filing- or priority date is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Older rights affect novelty under 'prior claims' approach (Swiss) vs 'whole contents' (EPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Swiss law (Art.7a PatG) treats unpublished earlier national/european/international filings as novelty-destroying only by their patent claims and only if they resulted in a valid patent ('prior claims approach'), whereas EPO practice applies 'whole contents' approach where the entire content can count as prior art irrespective of resulting patent grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Switzerland the older patent need not still be in force when attacking novelty; differences between jurisdictions affect novelty analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legally equivalent modes of disclosure but evidentiary differences (written/oral/use/other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure may occur by written description, oral description, (non-secret) use, or in any other way; legally these modes are equivalent, but differ in evidentiary strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dated published documents are generally stronger evidence than witness testimony or use; Swiss view: Internet publication is a special case of written disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age of disclosure: irrelevant for novelty but may affect inventive step evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Age of a disclosure does not matter for novelty — any identical older disclosure destroys novelty. For inventive step, very old publications may be disregarded if they have not influenced the technical field (forgotten).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swiss jurisprudence may ignore ancient publications that had no influence; EPO tends to include old documents but may view large time gaps as indicator of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of foreign/local place: not relevant (global accessibility suffices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether disclosure took place in another country does not prevent it from being prior art; absolute global novelty is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of whether disclosure was accidental or intentional abroad are therefore largely moot under absolute novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal elements: source of disclosure (applicant or third party) generally irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not matter who disclosed the information — a disclosure by the applicant is as novelty-destroying as by any other person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switzerland has no general grace period; narrow statutory exceptions (Art.7b PatG) exist for certain 'harmless disclosures' within six months before filing (obvious abusive disclosures to the applicant's detriment, and displays at recognized exhibitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality agreements do not negate that a disclosed information becomes prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A confidentiality obligation does not make a disclosure un-happened; published information becomes part of the state of the art even if the disclosing person was under a duty of confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the confidentiality was breached, the applicant may mitigate harm by filing a patent application within statutory grace/exception windows (e.g., Art.7b) where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for reverse engineering/analysis as disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure by putting a product on the market can be novelty-destroying if additional measures like demontage or analysis are (a) foreseeable and (b) of moderate effort for the skilled person, enabling them to obtain the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novelty can only be discovered after destructive analysis, Swiss case law may treat simple placing on the market as not novelty-destroying; EPO case law treats effort irrelevant (even destructive analysis can make the product prior art). Consider whether the skilled person had reason to suspect novelty (e.g., advertising).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic/paper equivalence: screen output and stored electronic info considered published if publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: A screen (visual interface) is a paper substitute for disclosure purposes; electronically stored and publicly retrievable information should be treated as published like a book in a public library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No specific requirements compared to other forms of disclosure so long as accessibility is unrestricted; various forms of network communication are treated similarly if accessible to the public. E-mails to specific addressees are not public unless made generally accessible by the provider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encryption, passwords and paywalls as access restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Encryption and passwords count as electronic keys; if access is restricted to a defined circle, the information is confidential. Paywalled (fee-required) information can be obtained by anyone paying the fee and thus is not confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If encrypted information is cracked and published by misuse, that misuse may produce a prior publication effect; search engines index only publicly accessible content and thus are not a confidentiality issue per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet disclosure: place of 'perception' vs server location, but accessibility suffices for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: For Internet postings, the 'place' could be considered where the disclosure is perceived (where access occurs) rather than the server location; however, for absolute novelty it suffices that the information can be arbitrarily retrieved anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Server location is less relevant; the crucial point is public retrievability without restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timestamp and evidence concerns for electronic disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic dates/timestamps are not always trustworthy; the identification of the disclosure date on the web is uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certified (trusted) archives would be desirable for proof; nevertheless, existing burden-of-proof rules should remain (the party alleging prior publication must prove it). Courts should evaluate reliability; no special stricter evidentiary standard for Internet disclosures is recommended since different standards would create legal uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: No different grades of proof by disclosure medium
rubrics_metrics.description: There should not be different evidentiary standards for different disclosure media; uniform handling of proof is needed for legal certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although electronic information may be more easily manipulated, this affects reliability evaluation but does not justify separate proof rules; the same proof rules as for other disclosure types should apply.
